<dialog> Dialog box

The <dialog> element represents a dialog box or other interactive component such as a confirmation prompt, an alert, a subwindow or a modal overlay. It is hidden by default and is shown with the open attribute or, preferably, with the JavaScript methods show() (non-modal) and showModal() (modal). A modal dialog blocks interaction with the rest of the page, is displayed on top of everything else, and can be closed with the Escape key.

<fencedframe> Fenced frame (experimental)

The <fencedframe> element embeds another HTML page in a way that is even more isolated than an <iframe>: the embedded page cannot communicate with the embedding page, and the URL is chosen through privacy-preserving APIs rather than given directly. It is part of the Privacy Sandbox proposals for showing personalised advertisements without cross-site tracking. It is not yet a standard and is only available in Chromium browsers.

<hgroup> Heading group

The <hgroup> element groups a heading (<h1>-<h6>) with one or more <p> elements that contain a subtitle, alternative title, tagline or other secondary text. It tells the browser that the paragraphs belong to the heading rather than being ordinary content.

<main> Main content

The <main> element represents the dominant content of the <body>: the content that is directly related to, or expands upon, the central topic of the page or the central function of the application. It excludes content repeated across pages such as the site header, navigation, sidebars, search box, logo and footer.

<menuitem> Menu item (obsolete)

The <menuitem> element represented a command in a <menu type="context">, letting a page add custom items to the browser's right-click menu. Only Firefox implemented it; it was removed from the standard in 2017 and from Firefox in 2020. Build custom menus with lists, buttons and JavaScript (or the popover attribute) instead.

<param> Object parameter (deprecated)

The <param> element defined a parameter for an <object> element, passing a name/value pair to the plug-in that displayed the object (for example the autoplay setting of a Flash movie). Since plug-ins no longer exist, the element serves no purpose; the Living Standard marks it deprecated and it is retained only for compatibility. It is a void element.

<picture> Picture (responsive image container)

The <picture> element contains zero or more <source> elements and exactly one <img> element, and lets the browser choose the most suitable image from several candidates. The browser examines each <source> in order and uses the first whose media query matches and whose type it supports; if none match it falls back to the <img>. The <img> element is required: it is what is actually displayed, and it carries the alt text, width, height, loading and other attributes.

<portal> Portal (experimental, abandoned)

The <portal> element was an experiment that embedded a preview of another page, like an iframe, with the ability to 'activate' it and navigate seamlessly into it with an animation. It was available only behind a flag in Chrome and the work has been superseded by the View Transitions API and prerendering with the Speculation Rules API. Do not use it.

<rb> Ruby base (deprecated)

The <rb> element explicitly marked the base text component of a ruby annotation, the text that the <rt> annotation is placed above. The Living Standard removed it because the base text can simply be written directly inside <ruby>. Browsers still support it.

<rtc> Ruby text container (deprecated)

The <rtc> element grouped several <rt> annotations so that a base text could have two layers of annotation (for example pronunciation above and meaning below). Only Firefox implemented it, and the Living Standard removed it. Nest two <ruby> elements for double-sided annotations.

<search> Search section

The <search> element represents a part of the document whose contents are search or filtering controls: a site search form, a filter panel in a product list, or the controls of a find-in-page feature. It has no visual effect; it exposes the 'search' landmark to assistive technology. It replaces the old pattern <form role="search">. The form itself still goes inside it.

<selectedcontent> Selected option display (customisable select)

The <selectedcontent> element is part of the customisable <select> proposal. Placed inside the <button> that sits at the start of a <select>, it mirrors the content of the currently selected <option>, so that rich option content (icons, colour swatches, descriptions) is shown in the closed control as well as in the open list. The browser clones the selected option's children into <selectedcontent> whenever the selection changes.

<slot> Shadow DOM slot

The <slot> element is a placeholder inside a web component's shadow tree that is filled with content from the light DOM (the markup written by the user of the component). A named slot receives children that have a matching slot attribute; the unnamed default slot receives all other children. Content inside the <slot> element itself is fallback content shown when nothing is slotted.

Part 4: Global Attributes

accesskey

Values: single character · Since: HTML 4.01

Defines a keyboard shortcut that activates or focuses the element. The key combination depends on the browser and operating system (usually Alt + key on Windows/Linux in Chrome and Edge, Alt + Shift + key in Firefox, Control + Option + key on macOS). Because these combinations often collide with browser and assistive-technology shortcuts, accesskey is rarely recommended; if used, document the shortcuts on the page.

<button accesskey="s">Save (Alt+S)</button>

autocapitalize

Values: off | none | on | sentences | words | characters · Since: Living Standard

Controls whether and how text input is automatically capitalised on virtual keyboards (phones and tablets). It has no effect on physical keyboards. Inherited by descendant editable elements.

<input name="username" autocapitalize="none">
<textarea autocapitalize="sentences"></textarea>

autocorrect

Values: on | off · Since: Living Standard

Controls whether the browser may automatically correct spelling in editable text. Originally a Safari extension, added to the Living Standard in 2024.

<input name="code" autocorrect="off">

autofocus

Values: boolean · Since: HTML5 (global since 2019)

Indicates that the element should receive focus as soon as the page loads (or the <dialog> it is in is shown). Only one element per document should have it. Use with care: moving focus automatically can disorient screen reader users and scrolls the page to the element.

<input name="q" type="search" autofocus>

class

Values: space-separated class names · Since: HTML 4.01

A list of the classes the element belongs to. Classes are the primary hook for CSS (selector .name) and for JavaScript (document.querySelectorAll('.name')). An element may have many classes and many elements may share a class. Class names are case-sensitive, should not start with a digit, and by convention use lowercase words joined with hyphens (kebab-case). Choose names that describe what the element is, not how it looks (product-card rather than red-box), so that the style can change without renaming.

<div class="card featured">...</div>
<style>.card { border: 1px solid #ccc; } .featured { border-color: gold; }</style>

contenteditable

Values: true | false | plaintext-only | (empty = true) · Since: HTML5

Makes the element's content editable by the user directly in the page, turning it into a basic rich-text editor. plaintext-only allows editing text but not formatting. The property is inherited: children of an editable element are editable unless they set contenteditable="false". Combine with the input event and the document.execCommand or Selection APIs to build editors.

<p contenteditable="true">Click here and edit this text.</p>

data-*

Values: any text · Since: HTML5

Custom data attributes. Any attribute whose name starts with data- is reserved for the page author's own data and is guaranteed never to be given a meaning by browsers. The value is available in JavaScript through element.dataset (data-user-id becomes dataset.userId) and in CSS through attr(). Use them to attach information to elements without misusing class or id.

<li data-product-id="42" data-price="120">Learn HTML</li>
<script>
  const li = document.querySelector('li');
  console.log(li.dataset.productId, li.dataset.price); // "42" "120"
</script>

dir

Values: ltr | rtl | auto · Since: HTML 4.01

The text direction of the element's content. ltr = left to right (English, French...); rtl = right to left (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Urdu); auto = let the browser decide from the first strongly directional character, useful for user-generated content. Set it on <html> for the whole page. It affects text alignment, the side on which bullets and scrollbars appear, and the order of table columns.

<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
<p dir="ltr">This English paragraph inside an Arabic page reads left to right.</p>
<input dir="auto">

draggable

Values: true | false · Since: HTML5

Whether the element can be dragged with the Drag and Drop API. Images and links are draggable by default; other elements need draggable="true". The value must be written explicitly (it is not a boolean attribute). Dragging fires dragstart, drag, dragend on the source and dragenter, dragover, drop on the target.

<div draggable="true" ondragstart="event.dataTransfer.setData('text', 'hello')">Drag me</div>

enterkeyhint

Values: enter | done | go | next | previous | search | send · Since: Living Standard

A hint about which label or icon to show on the Enter key of virtual keyboards, matching the action that pressing Enter will perform in this field.

<input type="search" enterkeyhint="search">
<textarea enterkeyhint="send"></textarea>

exportparts

Values: comma-separated part names (optionally name:alias) · Since: CSS Shadow Parts

In web components: re-exports parts from a nested shadow tree so that they can be styled from outside with the ::part() pseudo-element.

<my-dialog exportparts="header, footer:dialog-footer"></my-dialog>

hidden

Values: boolean | until-found · Since: HTML5

Indicates that the element is not (yet) relevant and should not be rendered. Browsers implement it as display: none, so any CSS that sets display on the element will override it (add [hidden] { display: none !important } to be safe). The value until-found keeps the content hidden but searchable with find-in-page and fragment links; the browser reveals it automatically when found. Do not use hidden to hide content only visually while keeping it for screen readers; use a visually-hidden CSS class instead.

<p hidden>Not shown.</p>
<section hidden="until-found">Revealed when the user searches for text inside it.</section>
<script>document.querySelector('p').hidden = false;</script>

id

Values: unique identifier · Since: HTML 4.01

A unique identifier for the element within the document. No two elements may share an id. It is used as the target of fragment links (href="#id"), by CSS (#id), by JavaScript (getElementById), by <label for>, by aria-labelledby and aria-describedby, by <input list>, by <output for>, by the form attribute and by <map name>. Ids are case-sensitive, must not contain spaces, and should start with a letter.

<h2 id="pricing">Pricing</h2>
<a href="#pricing">Jump to pricing</a>
<label for="email">Email</label> <input id="email">

inert

Values: boolean · Since: Living Standard (2022)

Makes the element and all its descendants inert: they cannot be focused, clicked, selected or found by find-in-page, and they are hidden from assistive technology. It is the tool for disabling everything behind a custom modal dialog or an open off-canvas menu. Native <dialog> showModal() applies inertness to the rest of the page automatically.

<main inert>Page content that cannot be interacted with while the menu is open</main>
<nav class="drawer">Menu</nav>

inputmode

Values: none | text | decimal | numeric | tel | search | email | url · Since: HTML5

A hint about which virtual keyboard to display when the element (an input, textarea or contenteditable) is focused. Unlike changing type, it does not change validation or the value: inputmode="numeric" on a text input shows a number pad but still accepts a postal code with a leading zero.

<input name="zip" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]*">
<input name="amount" inputmode="decimal">

is

Values: custom element name · Since: HTML5 / Custom Elements

Declares that a built-in element should behave like a customised built-in element defined with customElements.define(name, class, { extends: 'button' }). Not supported in Safari.

<button is="fancy-button">Click</button>

itemid, itemprop, itemref, itemscope, itemtype

Values: various · Since: HTML5 Microdata

Microdata attributes that embed machine-readable structured data (for example schema.org vocabularies) into the page for search engines. itemscope creates an item; itemtype gives its type URL; itemprop names a property; itemid gives a global identifier; itemref includes properties located elsewhere. JSON-LD in a <script type="application/ld+json"> is the more common approach today.

<div itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/Book">
  <span itemprop="name">Learn HTML</span> by
  <span itemprop="author">Sara</span>
</div>

lang

Values: BCP 47 language tag · Since: HTML 4.01

The language of the element's content. Language tags consist of a two-letter language code (en, ar, fr, de, es, zh, ja) optionally followed by a script (zh-Hans) and/or a region (en-GB, ar-EG, pt-BR). Set it on <html> for the page and on any element whose language differs. Browsers use it for hyphenation, quotation marks, font choice and spell checking; screen readers use it to switch voices; translation tools use it to decide what to translate. An empty value means the language is unknown.

<html lang="en">
<p>The word <span lang="ar">كتاب</span> means book.</p>

nonce

Values: cryptographic number used once · Since: CSP

A random token generated by the server for each response and listed in the Content-Security-Policy header, so that only the inline <script> and <style> elements carrying that nonce are allowed to run. Browsers hide the value from scripts after parsing.

<script nonce="r4nd0m">/* allowed by CSP 'nonce-r4nd0m' */</script>

part

Values: space-separated part names · Since: CSS Shadow Parts

In web components: names an element inside a shadow tree so that it can be styled from outside with the ::part(name) pseudo-element.

<!-- inside the shadow tree -->
<button part="confirm">OK</button>
<!-- outside -->
<style>my-dialog::part(confirm) { background: green; }</style>

popover

Values: auto | manual | hint | (empty = auto) · Since: Living Standard (2023)

Turns the element into a popover: hidden by default and displayed in the top layer (above everything else) when shown with a button that has popovertarget, or with showPopover()/togglePopover() in JavaScript. auto popovers close when the user clicks outside or presses Escape and only one is open at a time; manual popovers must be closed explicitly. Style the backdrop with ::backdrop and the open state with :popover-open.

<button popovertarget="menu">Menu</button>
<div id="menu" popover>
  <a href="/profile">Profile</a>
  <a href="/logout">Log out</a>
</div>

role

Values: ARIA role name · Since: WAI-ARIA 1.0

From WAI-ARIA: overrides or specifies the semantic role of the element for assistive technology, for example role="button", role="navigation", role="alert", role="tab". The first rule of ARIA is not to use it when a native element already has the right role: prefer <button> over <div role="button">. Use it for widgets HTML lacks (tabs, trees, comboboxes) and for landmarks in older browsers.

<div role="alert">Your order was placed.</div>
<ul role="tablist"><li role="tab" aria-selected="true">Details</li></ul>

aria-*

Values: various · Since: WAI-ARIA 1.0

From WAI-ARIA: a family of attributes that describe the state and properties of elements for assistive technology. The most used: aria-label (accessible name from a string), aria-labelledby (name from another element), aria-describedby (description), aria-hidden (hide from AT), aria-expanded (open/closed), aria-current (current item), aria-live (announce changes), aria-controls, aria-selected, aria-checked, aria-disabled, aria-required, aria-invalid, aria-haspopup, aria-pressed, aria-busy, aria-modal.

<button aria-label="Close" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="panel">×</button>
<div id="status" aria-live="polite"></div>

slot

Values: slot name · Since: DOM Standard

Assigns the element to a named <slot> inside the shadow tree of its parent custom element.

<user-card>
  <span slot="name">Ahmed</span>
</user-card>

spellcheck

Values: true | false · Since: HTML5

Whether the browser should check the spelling and grammar of the element's editable text. Browsers decide the default per element (usually on for textarea and contenteditable, off for input). Turn it off for codes, usernames and passwords. Note: some browsers send checked text to a remote service.

<textarea spellcheck="true"></textarea>
<input name="coupon" spellcheck="false">

style

Values: CSS declarations · Since: HTML 4.01

Inline CSS applied to this element only. Declarations are written as property: value pairs separated by semicolons, exactly as inside a style sheet rule but without the selector and braces. Inline styles have higher specificity than any selector and are hard to override, cannot use media queries or pseudo-classes, and are blocked by strict Content Security Policies, so prefer classes and a style sheet. Inline styles are convenient for quick tests and for values computed by JavaScript.

<p style="color: red; font-size: 1.2em; margin-bottom: 0">Inline styled paragraph</p>

tabindex

Values: integer · Since: HTML 4.01

Controls whether the element can be focused with the keyboard (Tab key) and in what order. tabindex="0" makes a normally non-focusable element (such as a div) focusable, in the natural document order. tabindex="-1" makes it focusable by script (element.focus()) but not by Tab; use it for the target of a skip link or a container that receives focus programmatically. Positive values (1, 2, 3...) force a custom order before all other elements and should be avoided because they make the page confusing. Interactive elements (links, buttons, form controls) are focusable without tabindex.

<div tabindex="0" role="button">Focusable custom control</div>
<main id="content" tabindex="-1">...</main>

title

Values: text · Since: HTML 4.01

Advisory information about the element, shown by most desktop browsers as a tooltip when the mouse rests on it. On <abbr> it holds the expansion; on <link rel=stylesheet> it names an alternate style sheet; on <iframe> it is the accessible name. Tooltips are not accessible to touch-screen or keyboard users and are read inconsistently by screen readers, so never put essential information only in title. Do not repeat the visible text in title; it produces double announcements.

<abbr title="World Health Organization">WHO</abbr>
<button title="Save (Ctrl+S)">Save</button>

translate

Values: yes | no | (empty = yes) · Since: HTML5

Whether the element's text and translatable attribute values should be translated when the page is localised by machine translation tools. Set translate="no" on brand names, code, and addresses.

<p>Buy it at <span translate="no">Book Store</span> today.</p>
<code translate="no">getElementById</code>

virtualkeyboardpolicy

Values: auto | manual · Since: VirtualKeyboard API

For editable elements: whether the virtual keyboard opens automatically on focus (auto) or only when the script calls navigator.virtualKeyboard.show() (manual).

<div contenteditable virtualkeyboardpolicy="manual"></div>

writingsuggestions

Values: true | false · Since: Living Standard (2024)

Whether the browser may offer writing suggestions (predictive text, autocomplete of sentences) in editable elements.

<textarea writingsuggestions="false"></textarea>

xml:lang, xml:base, xml:space

Values: various · Since: XHTML 1.0

XML attributes that only have meaning in XHTML documents served as XML. In HTML they are ignored (xml:lang must match lang if both are present).

<html xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" xml:lang="en" lang="en">

Every element accepts on* attributes whose value is JavaScript run when the event fires. Prefer addEventListener in scripts.

AttributeEventFires whenApplies to

onclickclickThe element was clicked with the primary button, tapped, or activated with Enter/Space on a button or link. The most used event attribute.All elements

onpause, onplay, onplayingpause, play, playingPlayback paused / play() called / actually started after buffering.audio, video

onprogressprogressPeriodic progress while downloading media.audio, video
onratechangeratechangePlayback speed changed.audio, video
onresetresetThe form was reset.form
onresizeresizeThe window was resized (on body); or an element resized (video). Use ResizeObserver for elements.body, video
onscrollscrollThe element or document scrolled.Scrollable elements, body
onscrollendscrollendScrolling finished.Scrollable elements, body

See the <body> entry.body
